etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English, from Old French dispenser, from Latin dispēnsāre (“to weigh out, pay out, distribute, regulate, manage, control, dispense”), frequentative of dispendere (“to weigh out”), from dis- (“apart”) + pendere (“to weigh”).

definitions.definition: To issue, distribute, or give out.

quote.citation: 1815 February 24, [Walter Scott], Guy Mannering; or, The Astrologer. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), Edinburgh:  […]  James Ballantyne and Co. for Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, […]; and Archibald Constable and Co., […], →OCLC:
quote.text: He is delighted to dispense a share of it to all the company.

quote.citation: 1955, William Golding, The Inheritors, Faber and Faber, published 2005, page 40:
quote.text: The smoky spray seemed to trap whatever light there was and to dispense it subtly.

definitions.definition: To apply, as laws to particular cases; to administer; to execute; to manage; to direct.

quote.citation: 1662, John Dryden, To the Lord Chancellor Hyde:
quote.text: While you dispense the laws, and guide the state.

definitions.definition: To supply or make up a medicine or prescription.
(particularly in canon law) To give a dispensation to (someone); to excuse.

quote.citation: 1603, Michel de Montaigne, chapter 34, in John Florio, transl., The Essayes […], book II, London:  […]  Val[entine] Simmes for Edward Blount […], →OCLC:
quote.text: After his victories, he often gave them the reines to all licenciousnesse, for a while dispencing them from all rules of military discipline […].

quote.citation: 1643, John Milton, Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce:
quote.text: Of evils the first and greatest is, that hereby a most absurd and rash imputation is fixt upon God and his holy Laws, of conniving and dispensing with open and common adultery among his chosen people; a thing which the rankest politician would think it shame and disworship, that his Laws should countenance; how and in what manner this comes to passe, I shall reserve, till the course of method brings on the unfolding of many Scriptures.

quote.citation: 1779–81, Samuel Johnson, "Richard Savage" in Lives of the Most Eminent English Poet
quote.text: He appeared to think himself born to be supported by others, and dispensed from all necessity of providing for himself.

quote.citation: 1849–1861, Thomas Babington Macaulay, chapter XI, in The History of England from the Accession of James the Second, volume (please specify |volume=I to V), London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, →OCLC:
quote.text: It was resolved that all members of the House who held commissions, should be dispensed from parliamentary attendance.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, obsolete) To compensate; to make up; to make amends.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book I, Canto III”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 30:
quote.text: One loving howre / For many yeares of sorrow can dispence

quote.citation: c. 1386–1390, John Gower, edited by Reinhold Pauli, Confessio Amantis of John Gower: Edited and Collated with the Best Manuscripts, volume (please specify |volume=I, II, or III), London: Bell and Daldy […], published 1857, →OCLC:
quote.text: His synne was dispensed with golde, wherof it was compensed(please add an English translation of this quotation)

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book II, Canto XII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: […]  what euer in this worldly state / Is sweet, and pleasing vnto liuing sense, / Or that may dayntiest fantasie aggrate, / Was poured forth with plentifull dispence  […]
